answer.rationale: The primary supply contract expires in 14 days with no auto-renew, so doing nothing is not a no-cost option; it is a forced interruption. The incumbent has already refused to reopen price, which forecloses the negotiate_terms direction under this cycle's 18% cut mandate. memory_c2 indicates the low-cost vendor can meet the mandate alone, that onboarding was quick last year, and that their invoicing stayed accurate — this is the one memory I need to pull the archived source for before committing, because the whole decision pivots on whether that earlier switch was genuinely clean or whether the consolidated record smoothed over friction. memory_c1 shows the incumbent delivered stability across two renewal cycles with no migration work, which is the real cost I am giving up by switching; I am weighing that but not pulling its archive because the decisive unknown is the low-cost vendor's track record, not the incumbent's. memory_c3 shows that adding a second source previously protected allocation during a shortage, but with the assembly line already at 94% of committed volume and no buffer, I cannot justify splitting volume across two suppliers this cycle; adding a second source also does not by itself meet the 18% cut, and I have capacity for exactly one sourcing decision. I flag delivery-risk sensitivity explicitly: if the archived record for memory_c2 reveals onboarding issues or invoicing disputes that the consolidated version understates, I would fall back to a short month-to-month bridge with the incumbent (the pattern memory_c5 shows is workable) rather than switch under deadline pressure. I am not deferring, because the contract expiry in 14 days makes defer_decision equivalent to accepting an unmanaged gap on the primary supply line.
